headline.coal_ash_comparison_note: A typical coal plant produces ~90 kg of fly + bottom ash per MWh electrical. A typical LWR produces ~3 g of spent fuel per MWh. Coal ash contains uranium and thorium at concentrations a few times higher than average crustal rock, and the absolute radioactive release to the biosphere from coal-plant fly ash worldwide exceeds that from the routine operation of all civil nuclear plants combined (McBride et al., Science 1978).

categories.typical_contents: Contaminated soil, construction rubble from decommissioning, lightly-activated metal.
categories.disposal: Surface landfills with modest engineered barriers (e.g. CIRES in France, low-level trenches in the US).

categories.typical_contents: Protective clothing, lab equipment, ion-exchange resins, filters from normal operations.
categories.disposal: Shallow engineered facilities (10-30 m depth) with concrete barriers. Examples: LLW Repository (UK), El Cabril (Spain), Barnwell (US, now closed).

categories.typical_contents: Reactor internals (activated steel), spent fuel cladding hulls and end-fittings, sludges from fuel-pond operations.
categories.disposal: Intermediate-depth geological facilities (100-200 m). Currently interim storage in most countries; a handful of deep ILW repositories operate (e.g. WIPP in the US for transuranic waste).

categories.typical_contents: Spent nuclear fuel (direct disposal) or vitrified reprocessing residues. The uranium-plutonium-fission-product mixture.
categories.disposal: Deep geological repositories (400-1000 m) in stable rock formations. As of 2026, only Finland's Onkalo is licensed for operational emplacement; Sweden's Forsmark is under construction.

global_stockpile_2023.notes: Cumulative since the start of commercial nuclear in the 1950s. All of it fits in a volume roughly equal to a football pitch stacked 10 m high: ~56,000 m3 of solid heavy-metal-equivalent, though the dry-cask storage footprint is several times larger due to shielding and spacing.

size_comparison.description: All high-level waste ever produced by commercial nuclear power could fit on a single American football field stacked about 10 meters high. For comparison, the world burns about 8 billion tonnes of coal per year, producing ~800 million tonnes of fly ash — enough to fill roughly 1000 Empire State Buildings annually.

deep_geological_repositories.name: Onkalo (Olkiluoto)
deep_geological_repositories.notes: First operational deep geological HLW repository in the world. Uses copper-canister KBS-3 design.

deep_geological_repositories.name: Cigeo (Bure)
deep_geological_repositories.notes: Clay host rock (low permeability) rather than crystalline rock.

deep_geological_repositories.name: WIPP
deep_geological_repositories.status: Operating since 1999 (transuranic defence waste only, not HLW)
deep_geological_repositories.planned_capacity_tonnes_hm: TRU waste; not for commercial HLW
deep_geological_repositories.notes: Only operating deep geological repository in the US, but for Cold-War-legacy weapons waste, not commercial spent fuel. Commercial US HLW remains in interim storage awaiting a permanent site after the Yucca Mountain project was defunded in 2011.

deep_geological_repositories.name: KBS-3 (concept)
deep_geological_repositories.country: Concept used by Finland and Sweden
deep_geological_repositories.notes: Multi-barrier system: spent fuel in copper canister, embedded in bentonite clay, emplaced in granite 400-500 m deep. Engineered barriers designed to contain radionuclides for >100,000 years.

reprocessing_status.description: Reprocessing separates uranium and plutonium from spent fuel to reuse as MOX fuel. Reduces HLW volume by ~75%% and radioactivity by ~90%% over 1000 years, but generates additional ILW streams and creates a weapons-proliferation concern.
reprocessing_status.proliferation_concern: The 1977 US decision to halt reprocessing for civil use was driven by non-proliferation policy, not economics.
